title: Loving animals
hook: Francis preaches to the birds (Little Flowers 16); Buddhists and Jains stress not harming

segments.voice: Yesterday, loving strangers. Your line was the stranger. Did a smile go to someone you'll never see again? Today, love crosses one more line, past our own kind entirely. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

A man in a rough patched habit is walking along a road in Italy with his companions when he notices trees full of birds and a field full of more. He tells his friends to wait. Then he walks into the field and starts preaching. To the birds. The story says they don't scatter. They stay, and listen, and don't fly off until he gives them his blessing. It's one of the stories gathered in The Little Flowers of Saint Francis. It could be read as a charming legend and nothing more. Today: what Francis actually says to the birds, and two other paths that take animals seriously too.
screen: `A FIELD FULL OF BIRDS.` → `HE STARTS PREACHING.` → `THEY STAY AND LISTEN.`

segments.voice: First, Francis and his sisters the birds. In the Little Flowers, Francis addresses them as his little sisters. Most of his sermon isn't about their faults. He reminds them how much they've been given: feathers to wear, the air to fly in, rivers and springs to drink from, and food they never had to sow or reap. So, he tells them, beware of ingratitude, and praise your Creator. In that story, the birds aren't scenery. They're fellow creatures with their own reasons to give thanks. Second, a righteous man regardeth his beast. The book of Proverbs puts it in one short line: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." Here, how someone treats an animal in their care isn't a side issue. It's part of what it means to be righteous. Third, the Jain care for small lives. In the Jain tradition, ahimsa, not harming, reaches all the way down to the smallest living things. The Acaranga Sutra, a Jain scripture, teaches that all beings love life and dislike pain, so none should be harmed. Some Jain monks and nuns carry a soft broom to sweep insects gently from where they're about to step or sit. Buddhists, too, place not harming living beings at the very start of their precepts. Fourth, gentleness, small and daily. None of this requires a field of birds. It might be slowing down for a dog on a leash, carrying a spider outside instead of crushing it, filling the water bowl before your own coffee. Francis called them sisters. That one word can change how a person walks past a pigeon.
screen: `FRANCIS AND HIS SISTERS THE BIRDS.` · `A RIGHTEOUS MAN REGARDETH HIS BEAST.` · `THE JAIN CARE FOR SMALL LIVES.` · `GENTLENESS, SMALL AND DAILY.` · then, large: `SISTER BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Let an animal come to mind. A pet beside you, a bird outside the window, a dog from childhood, even an ant on the counter. Breathe, and see it simply as a living thing: breathing too, wanting to stay alive, avoiding pain. Then do what Francis did in the field: go through what this creature has been given. Fur or feathers or a shell. Air, water, food it found. A way of moving that belongs to it. Name each gift silently, the way he named theirs, and let the creature be a little sister or brother for the length of the sit. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this creature. The bell holds the time.
Loving animals. Care that reaches past our own kind, the way Francis called the birds his sisters and the Jain path refuses to harm even the smallest life. Today's word.
Your line: sister birds. Today, be gentle with one animal on purpose: a pet, a stray, a bird, an insect you carry outside instead of swatting. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Some Catholic and other Christian churches hold a blessing of animals on Saint Francis's feast day; Jains practice ahimsa toward all living beings, and some Jain monks and nuns sweep their path to avoid harming insects; Buddhists take a precept to refrain from harming living beings.

notes: Audit pass (serious): Little Flowers ch. 16 has Francis warn the birds to beware the sin of ingratitude, so 'he doesn't lecture them about behaving' and 'doesn't preach morals' overstated the text. Teach, myth and trapdoor now include the warning.

Little Flowers ch. 16 is paraphrased: Francis tells companions to wait, preaches to the birds as 'my little sisters', lists feathers, air, waters and food they don't sow or reap, tells them to praise their Creator, and the birds stay until blessed. Confirm against a standard edition; no translation is quoted.
Acaranga Sutra: confirm the section reference for the teaching that all beings are fond of life and dislike pain (Jacobi 1884 places it in Book 1, Lecture 2, Lesson 3).
The soft broom (rajoharana) carried by some Jain monks and nuns: confirm wording, and that 'some' is fair across Svetambara and Digambara practice.
'Buddhists place not harming living beings at the very start of their precepts' refers to the first of the five precepts; confirm.
howItsDone mentions blessings of animals on Saint Francis's feast day in 'some' churches; confirm.

Editor pass: replaced the practice's loving-kindness phrases (the same wishing method as 857, 858 and 863 nearby) with Francis's own move, naming what a creature has been given; changed 'rough brown habit' to 'rough patched habit', since the Little Flowers chapter gives no color.
'a road in Italy' is general; the Little Flowers names places near Bevagna/Cannara, which the script leaves out.
